statement: A pizza shop offers 6 different vegetable toppings and 5 different meat toppings. A customer chooses 4 different toppings, including at least one vegetable topping and at least one meat topping. How many different choices are possible?

choices.misconception: I removed the choices with only vegetable toppings but forgot to remove the choices with only meat toppings.
I removed the choices with only meat toppings but forgot to remove the choices with only vegetable toppings.
I counted every choice of 4 toppings from 11 and ignored the condition.
I picked one vegetable, one meat and then any two others, $6 \times 5 \times \binom{9}{2}$, which counts the same choice several times.

hints: Count all selections of 4 toppings from 11, then subtract the selections that are all vegetable or all meat. This is complementary counting.
There are $\binom{11}{4} = 330$ selections, $\binom{6}{4} = 15$ all vegetable and $\binom{5}{4} = 5$ all meat.

solutions.reliable: All selections of 4 from 11 toppings: $\binom{11}{4} = 330$. The bad ones use only one kind: all vegetable $\binom{6}{4} = 15$, all meat $\binom{5}{4} = 5$. So $330 - 15 - 5 = 310$. Check by cases: 1 vegetable and 3 meat $6 \times 10 = 60$; 2 and 2: $15 \times 10 = 150$; 3 and 1: $20 \times 5 = 100$; total $310$. The transferable idea: 'at least one of each' is usually easiest as everything minus the selections that miss a kind.

whyOnTest: 'At least one of each' invites an overcount by fixing one of each first; the complement gives a clean answer in one step.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
